pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of the name ‌is **/ˈɡnoʊi/** — English ‌approximation of the ​Woiwurrung original[^1].

The closest ​modern approximation is: 'GNOH-wee' ​— stress the ​first syllable, keep the ​final vowel bright and ‌short, and avoid ​turning the first vowel ​into an English diphthong. ‌Some renderings soften the ​initial cluster toward ‌'NOH-wee'.

Because the ASCII ​form *gnowee* already encodes ‌the same consonants ​and vowels that the ​restoration uses, the name ​is a plain ​restoration. No stress mark, ​length mark, or distinctive ‌letter is added. ​The Woiwurrung language itself ‌was unwritten before colonization, ​and colonial transcriptions ‌do not record phonemic ​length or tone for ‌this name. The ​restoration therefore gives the ‌standard scholarly citation form ​rather than a ​phonetic transcription with additional ‌diacritics[^2].

Because Gnowee belongs ‌to an oral tradition, ‌the reconstructed pronunciation ​offered here is a ​scholarly romanization rather than ‌a phonetic record ​of a living speaker. ​The sounds of the ‌original language include ​phonemes that English does ​not distinguish, and early ‌recorders used inconsistent ​English-based spellings. PuniCodex therefore ‌treats the capitalized scholarly ​form **Gnowee** as ​the reference spelling, while ​noting that the ASCII ​form represents the ‌same romanized sequence. This ‌is why the name ​is a plain ‌restoration: the restoration recovers ​the proper-noun convention of ​the name without adding ‌a diacritic or ‌special letter that the ‌original ASCII string could ‌not carry.

domains.body:
Gnowee ​is the ‌sun ‌itself understood ​as a ​searching ​mother. Her ​domain ​therefore includes ‌solar ​light, the ​cycle of ‌day ​and night, ‌the ​moral obligations ‌attached ​to fire, ​and the ​connection ​between grief ​and ‌cosmic motion. ​In ‌Wurundjeri cosmology ​she ‌is not ​an abstract ‌celestial ​power but ‌a ​person with ​a ‌continuing story: ‌every sunrise ‌is ​the relighting ​of ‌her bark ​torch, ​every sunset ‌its guttering, ​every ​night the ‌pause ​while she ‌gathers ​more fuel.

​The domain ​of ​**Gnowee** is ‌best ‌understood within ​the ‌specific country ​of the ​Wurundjeri-willam: ‌the river ‌flats, ‌forests, and ‌volcanic ​plains of ‌the Melbourne ​region. ​The myth ​encodes ‌practical knowledge ​about ​fire management, ​child ‌supervision, and ​food gathering, ​as ​well as ‌a ​metaphysics in ‌which ​human emotion ‌can reshape ​the ‌heavens. Contemporary ‌Wurundjeri ​educators present ​the ​story as ​both cultural ‌heritage ‌and ecological ​teaching[^3].

mythology.body:
The ​central myth ‌of Gnowee ‌is the ​story ​of the ​woman who ​became the ​sun. In ‌the ​time before ​light, Gnowee ‌left her ​son ‌sleeping while ​she went ‌out to ​dig yams. ​She ​wandered too ​far, and ​when she ‌turned ​back she ‌could no ​longer find ‌her ​camp. To ‌search for ​him she ‌made a ​great ​torch of ‌bark, climbed ‌into the ‌sky, ​and began ​to travel ‌across it. ​That torch ​is ‌the sun; ​she carries ​it still.

‌The ​myth explains ‌not only ​the origin ​of ​the sun ​but also ‌its movement. ‌Gnowee cannot ​rest ‌until she ​finds her ​son, so ‌she ‌travels continuously ‌across the ‌sky. When ​the torch ‌burns ​low she ​stops to ​kindle a ‌fresh ​one, and ​that interval ​is night. ‌At ​dawn she ​lifts the ​new torch ‌and the ​search ‌resumes. The ​narrative thus ‌binds cosmology ​to ‌maternal grief, ‌fire technology ​to daily ​routine, and ​the ​sky to ‌the moral ‌landscape of ​country[^1].

overview.body:
**Gnowee** ​(*gnowee*) — ‌Sun Goddess ‌· The ​sun-woman who ​lost her ​son underground ​— belongs ​to the ‌Aboriginal tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Sun ‌Goddess". The ​name means ‌"The sun"[^1].

​**Gnowee** is ​the sun ​of the ​Wurundjeri people. ​In the ‌Kulin telling ​she was ‌once a ​woman who ‌went up ​into the ‌sky carrying ​a ‌bark torch, ​searching for ​the child ‌she had ‌lost in ‌the eternal ​darkness below. ​Her daily ‌journey across ​the heavens ​is that ‌search still ​in progress: ​when her ‌torch burns ​bright, the ‌world is ​day; when ​it dims ​and gutters, ​evening comes; ‌when she ‌stops to ​rekindle it, ‌night falls. ​She is ​therefore light-giver, ‌wanderer, and ‌bereaved mother ‌at ‌once.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical scholarly ​spelling **Gnowee** ​and serves ​its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/gnowee/). The ​displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description computed ​from the ​displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *gnowee* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ‌special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Gnowee** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "The ​sun"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Gnowee** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *gnowee* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

original-script.body:
No ​indigenous ‌writing ‌system is ​securely ​attested ​for ​individual ​aboriginal names. ‌The ​form ​shown ‌is ​a ‌modern scholarly ​transliteration.[^1]

‌The ​form ​**Gnowee** ​is therefore ​a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​rather ‌than ​an attested ‌ancient ​spelling; ‌it ​encodes ‌the reconstructed ​sound ​of ‌the ‌name ‌for ​modern use, ​and ‌no ​mark ​in ‌it is ​decorative.

​The ‌Woiwurrung ​language ‌was ​not written ​before ​colonization. ​The ‌name ‌survives in ​Latin ‌transcription, ​most ​commonly ‌spelled ‌*Gnowee*. The ‌PuniCodex ‌restoration ​capitalizes ‌the ​initial letter ​as ​a ‌proper ​name. ​No ​additional diacritics ‌or ​special ​letters ​are ‌used, because ​the ‌surviving ​scholarly ‌sources ​do ‌not record ‌distinctive ​phonemic ​length ​or ​stress marks ‌for ‌this ​name.

sources.citation: Massola, Aldo, Bunjil's Cave: Myths, Legends and Superstitions of the Aborigines of South-East Australia, Lansdowne Press, 1968.

meditation.body:
Gnowee ​invites meditation ‌on ‌the inseparability ​of ​love and ​loss. ​The sun ​rises ‌not because ​it ​is a ‌machine ​but because ‌a ​mother is ‌still ​looking. That ​reading ​transforms the ​sky ​from a ‌clock ​into ‌a story: ​every ‌dawn is ​the ‌relighting of ​a ‌torch, every ​noon ​the height ‌of ‌a search, ‌every ​dusk the ​guttering ‌of a ​flame ​that will ‌be ​renewed.

There ​is ‌also a ​lesson ‌about fire. ​In ​the myth, ​fire ​is not ‌stolen ‌or given; ​it ‌is carried. ​It ​must be ‌gathered, ‌tended, and ‌passed ‌on. The ​sun ‌is therefore ​the ​largest campfire, ​and ‌the ​obligations that ​govern ​a small ‌fire ​on country ​scale ​up to ‌the ​cosmos itself. ‌To ​remember Gnowee ‌is ​to remember ‌that ‌light is ​labor ​and that ​care ​can outlast ‌even ‌the longest ​night.[^1]

sources.citation: Massola, Aldo, Bunjil's Cave: Myths, Legends and Superstitions of the Aborigines of South-East Australia, Lansdowne Press, 1968.
